The early life stages of Unio tigridis are characterized by a dramatic size increase from the moment of birth. Newly released glochidia, the parasitic larval stage, measure only 0.02 centimeters [Lb = 0.02 centimeters] in shell length at birth. After an obligatory period of attachment to a fish host, during which the larva undergoes metamorphosis, the juvenile mussel excysts and settles onto the riverbed. The shell length at settlement is recorded as 0.03 centimeters , only marginally larger than the birth size but representing a critical ecological transition to a free-living, benthic existence. This minute size at settlement imposes severe constraints on the juvenile's ability to forage and avoid predation.

As the juvenile enters its period of rapid somatic growth, it will gradually approach its ultimate shell length. This maximum size, typical of a fully grown adult, has been determined to be 6.9 centimeters [Li = 6.9 centimeters]. Achieving this length requires several years of consistent filter-feeding in productive habitats. The onset of reproductive capability, or puberty, is linked to a specific body size rather than a strict chronological age, a common pattern among bivalves. Based on morphological studies, the shell length at puberty for this species is 2 centimeters [Lp = 2 centimeters] estimated at, a threshold that signals the reallocation of resources from somatic growth toward gametogenesis.

Reproductive output in freshwater mussels is often quantified under controlled laboratory conditions. Measurements of spawning activity in related species can provide useful comparative data for Unio tigridis. At a stable water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the annual reproductive output for an individual of Unio tigridis measuring 4 centimeters in shell length has been estimated at approximately 12,000 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 12,000 offspring per year]. This value was derived from fecundity assessments of a congeneric species, Unio tumidiformis, under similar thermal regimes. It is important to note that this rate may vary significantly based on local food availability and the physiological condition of the adult female.

Survivorship and longevity are critical parameters for understanding the population dynamics of long-lived freshwater mussels. For Unio tigridis, a comprehensive mark-recapture study conducted at 18 °C [T = 18 °C] yielded a maximum lifespan estimate of 4015 days [am = 4015 days]. This exceptional longevity, equating to roughly 11 years, underscores the species' slow pace of life, characterized by delayed maturity and a low annual reproductive output relative to body size. The shell accretes new material continuously, with growth rings providing a reliable record of age and seasonal conditions, data which confirm that most individuals do not reach this extreme age due to high juvenile mortality.

The interplay between size at settlement and eventual adult size dictates fundamental aspects of mussel ecology. Because the shell length at birth is a mere 0.02 centimeters [Lb = 0.02 centimeters], the journey to the adult length of 6.9 centimeters [Li = 6.9 centimeters] represents a 345-fold increase in linear dimension, a remarkable scaling feat for a sedentary filter feeder. This growth trajectory is strongly regulated by temperature; for example, the 4015-day maximum lifespan (4015 days) [am = 4015 days] was observed under stable thermal conditions at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. Furthermore, the annual reproductive output of roughly 12,000 offspring per year [Ri = roughly 12,000 offspring per year] measured at 4 centimeters shell length highlights the energetic demands of reaching the 2-centimeter puberty threshold (2 centimeters) [Lp = 2 centimeters] before initiating reproduction.
